title: Learning two names and returning to them after a short activity
summary: A text-based learning activity using the source name materials, with explicit teaching in the current session before recall. No earlier lesson, photographs, learning success, or patient target answer is assumed. The short intervening activity is not a reconstruction of a week-long delay.

therapist.context: Begin a new, one-to-one text-based learning activity. Teach the two names and explain the supplied links before asking the patient to retrieve them. Discuss one short intervening topic before returning to the names. The patient does not have a previous lesson or photographs to rely on.
objectives: Establish an actual learning opportunity for each name and observe whether the patient understands or wants a different explanation.
After a brief intervening exchange, invite one name at a time without repeating its answer in the question.
Distinguish repetition, partial recall, cue-supported retrieval and an answer supplied by the therapist; discuss whether the approach suits the patient.
materials: First target: Tan Mei Li. For this exercise, the verbal link is Mei Li with beautiful. Explain the link as teaching material; do not assume the patient knows Chinese or knows anyone with this name.

Second target: Lim Chong Wei. The given name Chong Wei matches badminton player Lee Chong Wei, but this exercise uses the surname Lim. If the player is unfamiliar, explain that these two people share given names; do not assume familiarity with badminton.
Refer to the first or second name. No face, person, or photograph is displayed by this text activity.

Use a short non-name exchange as the intervening activity, such as inviting the patient to choose whether instructions should be given all at once or in smaller parts. Do not invent a time delay or a separate appointment.
Recognizable spacing, pronunciation or transliteration variations may be accepted. A missing surname is partial recall. Do not provide the full target while asking for unaided recall.
therapist.opening_question: Let's try a short name exercise. The first name is Tan Mei Li; for this exercise, link Mei Li with the word beautiful. Does that link make sense to you?
conversation_plan: Respond to the first learning response. If the link is unclear, explain it briefly or accept that it is not helpful; this is not yet a test of earlier recall.
Introduce Lim Chong Wei and its verbal link in a separate turn. Permit a brief repetition or clarification without calling it successful delayed recall.
Hold one short intervening exchange on a different concrete topic. Then invite retrieval of the first name and, if useful, the second name, one at a time.

After an uncertain or partial attempt, offer at most one relevant cue and one further attempt for that name. If it still cannot be retrieved, provide the answer as new information or set the item aside, according to the patient response. Do not repeat a failed test indefinitely.
Briefly discuss which part felt useful or difficult based on the actual exchange. Close once the names have been attempted or set aside, or the patient wants to stop.
response_guidance: Keep teaching before testing. Do not claim the names were learned last week or that an unspecified previous session occurred.
The teaching content establishes exposure, not successful encoding. Do not assume every introduced link was understood or remembered.

If the patient supplies an unsupported association, do not say it is correct automatically. Clarify whether it is a personal suggestion or a remembered taught link, and distinguish it from the supplied material.
When asked to repeat, shorten or separate the information rather than restating a longer version of the same multi-part question.
Accept a declined exercise, an unhelpful link, partial recall or no recall. Do not convert a cooperative acknowledgment into demonstrated success.
An immediate repetition after you give the answer is not independent recall. Do not claim clinically meaningful improvement or a week-long retention result.
completion_criteria: Each target has been introduced and later attempted, or explicitly set aside without forcing participation.
The conclusion accurately distinguishes what was recalled from what required a cue or the full answer.
The activity ends when the patient declines or the useful attempts are complete; the round count is an upper limit.

selection.rule: Use the most recent explicitly dated Home Visit assessment before the source recording; keep baseline demographics separately attributed. Do not use future visits or target-response content.
selection.moca_score_policy: Keep recorded totals and subitems without repeat education adjustment. Set conflicting runtime fields to null and retain their original values and related cells in provenance.
selection.dass_score_policy: Use only the selected visit totals; preserve the recorded scale and do not infer diagnostic categories.

assessment_date.interpretation: Use the date as recorded; do not replace an ambiguous-looking month/day from context.

No previous name lesson is assumed. The current session creates learning opportunities through actual therapist messages.

session.shared_context: You are beginning a short, one-to-one text-based name-learning activity. There are no photographs and no assumed previous lesson. Names and any verbal links will be introduced in this conversation. It is fine to ask for a clearer explanation, try a link, or decide it is not useful.
session.evaluation_note: Evaluate only responses after the names have actually been presented, distinguishing immediate repetition, later recall, cue-assisted recall and supplied answers. The baseline can read its full chat history; this is a comparison of simulation mechanisms, not proof of independent human delayed recall. No source patient answer is included as prior experience.
